title: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings
body: Bare-nosed wombats leave neat cubes of dung, which they stack on rocks and logs to mark territory. A 2018 study found the cubes are shaped inside the intestine, where stiffer and more elastic bands of gut wall squeeze the contents into flat sides and corners.

title: A day on Venus outlasts its year
body: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west.

title: Cleopatra lived nearer the Moon landing than Giza
body: Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years after the Great Pyramid of Giza was built but only about 2,000 years before Apollo 11. Ancient Egypt lasted so long that its own pyramids were ancient history to her.

title: "Nice" once meant foolish
body: In medieval English, calling someone nice meant they were silly or ignorant. The word comes from Latin nescius, "not knowing", and drifted over centuries through meanings like shy and fussy before settling on pleasant.

title: Dolphins sleep with half a brain
body: Bottlenose dolphins rest one half of the brain while the other half stays awake. This lets them keep surfacing to breathe and stay alert to danger while they sleep.

title: Old windows are not slowly flowing glass
body: Some old panes are thicker at the bottom, but not because glass flows. Medieval glassmaking produced uneven sheets, and glaziers often fitted the thick edge at the bottom. At room temperature, glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably.

title: The ocean spot farthest from any land
body: Point Nemo in the South Pacific lies about 2,700 km from the nearest land. Space stations orbiting about 400 km up can pass closer to it than any person on dry ground.

title: Peanuts are not really nuts
body: Peanuts are legumes, members of the pea and bean family. Their flowers bend down and push into the soil, so the pods ripen underground rather than on a tree.

title: One fungus covers nearly ten square kilometres
body: A honey fungus in the Blue Mountains of Oregon is one individual spreading underground across almost ten square kilometres. Its threads creep through soil and tree roots, and it may be thousands of years old.

title: A metal that melts in your hand
body: Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a piece held in a warm hand slowly turns to liquid. Yet it stays liquid up to about 2,400 degrees, one of the widest liquid ranges of any element.

title: Kit Kats are lucky charms in Japan
body: Kit Kat sounds like 'kitto katsu', Japanese for 'you will surely win'. Students often receive the chocolate as a good-luck gift before exams.

title: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
body: In 1957 two American engineers, Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes, sealed two shower curtains together hoping to sell textured wallpaper. It flopped, and they later found success marketing it as packaging.

title: An octopus has three hearts
body: Octopuses have two hearts that pump blood through the gills and a third for the rest of the body. Their blood is blue, because it carries oxygen with a copper-based molecule rather than the iron-based haemoglobin in ours.

title: Twenty-three people make a shared birthday likely
body: In a group of just 23 people, there is a better than 50 per cent chance that two share a birthday. The trick is that it can be any pair, and 23 people form 253 different pairs.

title: Why the UK tax year starts in April
body: England's year once began on 25 March. When Britain skipped 11 days in 1752 to switch calendars, the tax year was moved to keep full-length years, and a later adjustment landed it on 6 April.

title: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
body: The statue is covered in thin copper sheets, which were a shiny reddish brown in 1886. Within about twenty years the copper had reacted with the air to form the green patina that now protects it.

title: Your stomach lining renews every few days
body: The cells lining the inside of your stomach are replaced every few days. Coated in protective mucus, they still take a battering from the strong acid, so the body constantly sheds old cells and grows new ones.

title: Why snowflakes have six arms
body: Snowflakes are six-sided because water molecules link up in a hexagonal pattern when they freeze. Each arm grows in almost identical conditions as the flake falls, so the arms tend to match.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec capital
body: Teaching was going on at Oxford by 1096, while the Mexica founded their city of Tenochtitlan around 1325. Europe's universities and the Aztec Empire belong to very different chapters of history, yet Oxford came first.

title: "Happy Birthday" began as a school greeting
body: The tune of Happy Birthday comes from "Good Morning to All", a song published by two American sisters, Mildred and Patty Hill, in 1893 for children to sing at the start of the school day.

title: Koalas have fingerprints like ours
body: Koala fingerprints are so similar to human ones, with loops and whorls, that even under a microscope they are hard to tell apart. The trait evolved independently, probably to help koalas grip branches and handle eucalyptus leaves.

title: You cannot hum with your nose pinched
body: Try humming a tune with your nose held shut: the sound soon stops. Humming keeps your mouth closed, so air must escape through your nose, and once both are blocked the airflow stops.

title: A whole country high in the mountains
body: Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa, and even its lowest point sits about 1,400 metres above sea level. That gives it the highest low point of any country.

title: Frankenstein began as a holiday ghost-story contest
body: During a cold, rainy summer in 1816 near Lake Geneva, Lord Byron challenged his friends to write ghost stories. The 18-year-old Mary Shelley came up with Frankenstein, published two years later.

title: A whole aspen forest can be one tree
body: Pando, a grove in Utah, looks like a forest but is a single quaking aspen. Its tens of thousands of trunks all grow from one shared root system and are genetically identical, making it one of the heaviest organisms known.

title: Sunsets on Mars are blue
body: Photos from NASA rovers show a bluish glow around the setting Sun on Mars. Fine Martian dust scatters blue light forward, close to the direction of the Sun, while the rest of the daytime sky looks butterscotch.

title: Fried chicken is a Christmas tradition in Japan
body: Many Japanese families eat KFC at Christmas thanks to a hugely successful 1974 advert, 'Kentucky for Christmas'. Christmas is not a religious holiday there, so the custom filled a gap.

title: Basketball began with peach baskets
body: James Naismith invented basketball in 1891 in Massachusetts, using peach baskets as goals. The baskets still had bottoms, so someone had to fetch the ball out after each score.

title: Fungi are closer relatives of animals than plants
body: Mushrooms may look like plants, but DNA shows fungi and animals share a more recent common ancestor. Like us, fungi cannot make their own food and must absorb it from their surroundings.

title: Sound races through water
body: Sound travels at about 1,500 metres per second in water, more than four times faster than in air. Water molecules are packed closely and resist being squeezed, so vibrations pass between them faster.

title: Sweden once had a 30 February
body: Sweden tried a gradual calendar switch from 1700 but botched it. To get back in step, it added an extra day in 1712, creating a unique 30 February.

title: A muscle is a "little mouse"
body: The word muscle comes from Latin musculus, meaning little mouse. Romans thought a flexing muscle rippling under the skin looked like a mouse scurrying beneath a cloth.

title: A shrimp snaps hard enough to flash
body: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw shut so fast it fires a jet of water that forms a bubble. When the bubble collapses it makes one of the loudest sounds in the sea, stunning prey, and briefly gives off a tiny flash of light.

title: Helium was found in the Sun first
body: In 1868 astronomers studying sunlight during an eclipse saw a yellow spectral line no known element made. It was named helium, from the Greek for Sun, and was only found on Earth in 1895.

title: Mammoths still lived when the pyramids were built
body: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. That is several centuries after the Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC.

title: Bananas are berries but strawberries are not
body: To a botanist, a banana counts as a berry because it grows from a single flower with one ovary. A strawberry does not, and the little "seeds" on its outside are each a tiny separate fruit.

title: You are taller in the morning
body: Most people are around a centimetre taller when they wake than at bedtime. During the day, gravity squeezes fluid out of the soft discs between the vertebrae, and lying down overnight lets them swell back.

title: Every well-shuffled deck is probably unique
body: A pack of 52 cards can be arranged in about 8 followed by 67 zeros ways. That is so many that a properly shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order no deck has ever been in before.

title: Two countries that are doubly landlocked
body: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are each surrounded only by other landlocked countries. To reach the sea from either, you must cross at least two borders.

title: The Post-it Note began as a failed glue
body: In 1968 a 3M chemist, Spencer Silver, made an adhesive too weak for ordinary use. Years later his colleague Art Fry used it to keep bookmarks in his hymn book, and the sticky note was born.

title: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
body: Hummingbirds can hover in one spot and even fly backwards. Their wings twist at the shoulder and trace a figure-of-eight, producing lift on both the forward and the back stroke, much as an insect's wings do.

title: Raindrops are not tear-shaped
body: Small raindrops are almost perfectly round, held by surface tension. Larger drops are flattened underneath by air resistance into a shape like a burger bun, and the biggest ones break apart.

title: Spaniards eat twelve grapes at midnight
body: On New Year's Eve people in Spain try to eat one grape with each of the twelve chimes at midnight. Each grape is said to bring luck for one month of the coming year.

title: A blue paint could cost more than gold
body: Ultramarine blue was made by grinding lapis lazuli, mined mainly in Afghanistan. In Renaissance Europe it could cost more than gold, so painters often saved it for the robes of the Virgin Mary.

title: Some bamboo grows nearly a metre daily
body: Certain bamboo species can grow close to a metre in a single day. Bamboo is a grass, and rather than adding new cells at the tip it stretches many segments at once, each already packed into the young shoot.

title: Microwaves do not cook from the inside out
body: Household microwaves penetrate only about a centimetre or so into most foods. The middle warms more slowly, by heat conducted inwards from the outer layers, which is why thick food is often still cold in the centre.

title: Russia's October Revolution happened in November
body: Russia still used the old Julian calendar in 1917, so the revolution of 25 October was 7 November elsewhere. The Bolsheviks switched to the Gregorian calendar a few months later.

title: Mozart wrote variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle"
body: The tune of Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is an old French song, "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman". Mozart wrote twelve piano variations on it; the English words come from a poem by Jane Taylor.

title: Most plants rely on underground fungal partners
body: The large majority of land plants have fungi growing in or around their roots. The fungal threads reach far into the soil and trade water and minerals for sugars the plant makes from sunlight.

title: Saturn is less dense than water
body: Saturn's average density is only about 0.7 grams per cubic centimetre, lower than water's 1. It is mostly hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements, so in an impossibly large bathtub it would float.

title: A war that lasted under an hour
body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 40 minutes of shelling, making it the shortest war on record. A British fleet bombarded the palace and the sultan's side quickly gave up.

title: Sherlock Holmes never says "Elementary, my dear Watson"
body: The famous line does not appear in any of Arthur Conan Doyle's stories. Holmes does say "elementary" and "my dear Watson", but never together; the phrase was popularised later.

title: Greenland sharks live for centuries
body: Greenland sharks grow about a centimetre a year in icy Arctic waters. Dating proteins in their eye lenses in 2016 suggested some are at least 270 years old, and possibly much older.

title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
body: On hot days the iron of the Eiffel Tower expands, making it more than 10 centimetres taller than in winter. The sunny side expands more than the shaded side, so the top also leans slightly away from the Sun.

title: A border that runs through living rooms
body: In the town of Baarle, Belgian enclaves sit inside the Netherlands and Dutch ones inside those. The border can cut through houses, and a home's nationality is traditionally decided by where its front door lies.

title: Volleyball was first called mintonette
body: William G. Morgan invented the game in 1895 as a gentler indoor sport than basketball. He called it mintonette, after badminton, before the name volleyball took over.

title: Babies have more bones than adults
body: A newborn has around 300 bones and bony parts, while an adult has 206. Many start separate and fuse as we grow, such as the plates of the skull and the bones at the base of the spine.

title: Bananas are very slightly radioactive
body: Bananas are rich in potassium, and a tiny fraction of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40. The dose from eating one is far too small to matter; your own body contains the same isotope.

title: Danes smash plates on friends' doors
body: On New Year's Eve some Danes throw old crockery at the doors of friends and family. A big pile of broken china outside your home means you are well loved.

title: The word "robot" comes from a play
body: "Robot" first appeared in Karel Čapek's 1920 Czech play R.U.R., about artificial workers. His brother Josef suggested it, based on robota, a Czech word for forced labour.

title: Flamingos are pink because of their food
body: Flamingo chicks hatch grey and only turn pink from eating algae and tiny shrimps rich in carotenoid pigments. The birds store these pigments in their feathers, so a flamingo on a poor diet slowly fades.

title: 0.999 recurring is exactly equal to 1
body: The number 0.999... with nines going on forever is not just close to 1, it is 1. One neat proof: one third is 0.333..., and three thirds are 0.999..., which must equal 1.

title: One Roman year lasted 445 days
body: To fix a calendar that had drifted months out of step with the seasons, Julius Caesar added extra months to 46 BC. Romans called it the 'year of confusion'.

title: Carrots were once purple and yellow
body: The first cultivated carrots, grown around Afghanistan, were mostly purple or yellow. The orange carrot we know today was developed largely by Dutch growers in the 16th and 17th centuries.

title: Some turtles breathe through their rear end
body: Australia's Fitzroy River turtle can take in much of the oxygen it needs from water drawn into its cloaca, the opening at the base of its tail. This lets it stay underwater for long periods.

title: Every rainbow is really a full circle
body: Rainbows are circles centred on the point directly opposite the Sun. From the ground the horizon cuts off the lower part, but from an aircraft or high mountain you can sometimes see the whole ring.

title: Darwin and Lincoln shared a birthday
body: Charles Darwin and Abraham Lincoln were both born on 12 February 1809, on opposite sides of the Atlantic. One reshaped biology, the other led the United States through its Civil War.

title: Velcro was inspired by a dog's walk
body: After a walk in the Alps, Swiss engineer George de Mestral found burrs stuck to his dog's fur. Under a microscope he saw tiny hooks catching on loops, and copied the idea. The name joins French velours and crochet.

title: Leafcutter ants are fungus farmers
body: Leafcutter ants of the Americas do not eat the leaves they carry. They chew them into a pulp to grow a fungus garden in their nest, and the fungus feeds their larvae. Ants were farming fungus millions of years before humans farmed anything.

title: Fizzy drink bubbles start on tiny flaws
body: Bubbles in a fizzy drink mostly form at scratches, dust or fibres in the glass, where gas can gather. That is why streams of bubbles rise from the same spots, and why sweets dropped in cola fizz wildly.

title: Australia is wider than the Moon
body: Mainland Australia stretches about 4,000 km from east to west. The Moon's diameter is only about 3,475 km, so it would fit across the continent.

title: The Olympics once gave medals for art
body: From 1912 to 1948 the Olympic Games held competitions in painting, sculpture, music, literature and architecture. The founder of the modern Games, Pierre de Coubertin, won a gold for a poem under a pen name.

title: One jellyfish can turn back its life
body: The tiny jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can, when stressed or injured, transform back into its early polyp stage and grow up all over again. In principle this lets it escape death from old age, though it still gets eaten or falls ill.

title: A sugar cube of neutron star weighs billions
body: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across. Its matter is so tightly crushed that a sugar-cube-sized piece would weigh around a billion tonnes on Earth.

title: Finland holds a wife-carrying championship
body: Every summer in Sonkajärvi, couples race over an obstacle course with one partner carried by the other. It is inspired by local legends about a 19th-century bandit called Rosvo-Ronkainen.

title: The brass saxophone is a woodwind
body: The saxophone, patented by the Belgian Adolphe Sax in the 1840s, has a brass body. It is classed as a woodwind because its sound is made by a single reed, just like a clarinet.

title: Your body faintly glows
body: Humans give off visible light, about a thousand times too weak for our eyes to detect. Japanese researchers photographed it in 2009 with very sensitive cameras; it comes from chemical reactions in the skin and peaks in the afternoon.

title: A cracking whip breaks the sound barrier
body: The crack of a whip is a small sonic boom. As the loop travels down the tapering whip, it speeds up until the tip moves faster than sound, about 343 metres per second in air.

title: September was once the seventh month
body: The names September to December come from the Latin for seven to ten. The early Roman year began in March, so these really were the seventh to tenth months.

title: A novel without the letter e
body: Georges Perec's 1969 French novel La Disparition contains no letter e at all. Even more remarkably, its English translation, A Void by Gilbert Adair, avoids the letter too.

title: Honeybees give directions by dancing
body: A forager honeybee that finds food performs a 'waggle dance' in the hive. The angle of the dance relative to vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle shows the distance. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding it.

title: One Swedish village named four elements
body: Yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium are all named after Ytterby, a village near Stockholm. Its quarry yielded unusual minerals in which chemists found several new elements.

title: Harvard is older than calculus
body: Harvard was founded in 1636, decades before Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz independently developed calculus in the 1660s to 1680s. Early students studied Latin, Greek and theology rather than modern maths.

title: Dimples make golf balls fly further
body: The dimples on a golf ball create a thin layer of turbulent air around it, which reduces drag. A dimpled ball flies much further than a perfectly smooth one.

title: Venus flytraps can count
body: A Venus flytrap only snaps shut when a trigger hair is touched twice within about 20 seconds, avoiding false alarms from raindrops. Research in 2016 showed it starts producing digestive enzymes only after about five touches.

title: Folding paper 42 times would reach the Moon
body: Each fold doubles the thickness, so a sheet 0.1 millimetres thick folded 42 times would be about 440,000 kilometres thick, beyond the Moon. In practice, paper becomes impossible to fold after only a handful of folds.

title: Alaska is the USA's farthest west and east
body: Alaska's Aleutian Islands cross the 180° line of longitude. Some lie in the Eastern Hemisphere, making Alaska both the westernmost and easternmost US state, as well as the northernmost.

title: A clue was once a ball of thread
body: "Clue" comes from clew, a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unwound a clew to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth, so following a clue came to mean solving a puzzle.

title: A fungus turns ants into puppets
body: In tropical forests a fungus infects carpenter ants and makes them climb a plant and clamp their jaws on a leaf vein. The fungus then grows out of the ant and showers spores on the ants below.

title: Ancient corals recorded shorter days
body: Growth bands in fossil corals about 400 million years old suggest a year then had roughly 400 days. Earth spun faster, so each day lasted about 22 hours; tidal friction has been slowing it ever since.

title: People chase a cheese down an English hill
body: At Cooper's Hill in Gloucestershire, competitors race a round of Double Gloucester cheese down a very steep slope. The first to the bottom wins the cheese.

title: Birds cannot feel the heat of chillies
body: Birds lack the receptor that makes capsaicin feel hot, so they happily eat chillies. That suits the plant: birds swallow the seeds whole and spread them, while mammals would chew and destroy them.

title: Male seahorses give birth
body: In seahorses the female places her eggs in a pouch on the male's belly. He fertilises them, supplies oxygen and nutrients, then after a few weeks pushes out dozens or hundreds of fully formed babies.

title: Popcorn pops because of steam
body: Each popcorn kernel holds a little water inside a tough hull. Heated to about 180 degrees Celsius, the water turns to high-pressure steam until the hull bursts and the starch puffs into foam.

title: Ethiopia's calendar has thirteen months
body: The Ethiopian calendar has twelve months of 30 days plus a short thirteenth month of five or six days. It also counts years differently, running about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian calendar.

title: A melted sweet led to the microwave oven
body: In the 1940s engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a sweet in his pocket melted. He realised microwaves could heat food, and his company Raytheon built the first microwave ovens.

title: Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors
body: When you feel cold or thrilled, tiny muscles pull each body hair upright, making goosebumps. In furrier mammals this fluffs up the coat to trap warm air or to look bigger, but on our thin hair it does almost nothing.

title: Moon footprints could last for ages
body: The bootprints left by Apollo astronauts may survive for millions of years. The Moon has no wind, rain or flowing water to wipe them away, only a very slow rain of tiny meteorites.

title: The Byzantines never called themselves Byzantine
body: People of the eastern empire ruled from Constantinople called themselves Romans until its fall in 1453. The label 'Byzantine' was popularised by Western scholars, notably Hieronymus Wolf in the 16th century.

title: Rodin's Thinker was first called The Poet
body: The famous figure began as part of Rodin's Gates of Hell, a doorway inspired by Dante's Divine Comedy, where it sat above the door and was called The Poet. Many think it was meant to show Dante pondering his great work.

title: Giraffes have as many neck bones as you
body: Despite its enormous neck, a giraffe has seven neck vertebrae, the same number as a human and almost every other mammal. Each giraffe vertebra is simply much longer, some over 25 centimetres.

title: Sunlight is ancient by the time it leaves
body: Energy made in the Sun's core takes tens of thousands of years or more to reach the surface, as light is absorbed and re-emitted countless times. Once out, it reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

title: Reno lies west of Los Angeles
body: Although Nevada is east of California, Reno is farther west than Los Angeles. California's coast curves south-east, so LA sits well to the east of much of the state.

title: A one-page piano piece lasting 18 hours
body: Erik Satie's Vexations is only a page long, but a note on it is often read as asking for 840 repetitions. When John Cage organised a full performance in 1963, a team of pianists took about 18 hours.

title: Young sunflowers follow the Sun
body: Growing sunflowers turn east to west during the day and swing back at night, guided by an internal clock. Once they bloom they stop and face east, which warms the flowers in the morning and attracts more bees.

title: Diamonds can burn
body: Diamond is pure carbon, so heated strongly in oxygen it burns to carbon dioxide like coal. In the 1770s Antoine Lavoisier burned diamonds with a giant magnifying lens to show this.

title: Iceland celebrates Christmas with a book flood
body: In Iceland it is a tradition to give books on Christmas Eve and spend the night reading. The pre-Christmas rush of new titles is called Jólabókaflóð, the 'Christmas book flood'.

title: Green Eggs and Ham uses just 50 words
body: Dr Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham after his publisher bet him he could not write a book using only 50 different words. He managed it and won the bet.

title: Some mushrooms glow in the dark
body: Over a hundred kinds of fungi give off a soft green light, once called 'foxfire'. In Japan, Mycena chlorophos lights up damp forests at night. The glow may attract insects that help spread spores.

title: Multiplying ones makes a perfect palindrome
body: Multiply 111,111,111 by itself and you get 12,345,678,987,654,321. The digits climb from 1 to 9 and back down because of the way the carries line up when long multiplication adds the columns.

title: Revolutionary France tried ten-hour days
body: After the Revolution, France introduced a calendar with ten-day weeks and days named after plants, animals and tools. For a while it even promoted decimal clocks with ten hours a day, but they never caught on.

title: The chess queen was once very weak
body: In early chess the queen's place was held by a counsellor that moved only one square diagonally. Around the late 15th century, probably in Spain, the queen gained her powerful sweeping moves.

title: Mantis shrimp see colour unusually
body: Mantis shrimp have more than ten types of colour receptor, compared with our three. Yet tests show they are poor at telling similar colours apart; they seem to recognise colours instantly instead of comparing signals as our brains do.

title: A fluffy cloud weighs hundreds of tonnes
body: A typical small cumulus cloud holds hundreds of tonnes of water in tiny droplets. It floats because the droplets are spread through a huge volume of air and rising air currents keep them aloft.

title: Not holy, not Roman, not an empire
body: Voltaire joked that the Holy Roman Empire was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'. By his day it was a loose patchwork of German-speaking states with an elected emperor and little central power.

title: There is no horse in a nightmare
body: The "mare" in nightmare has nothing to do with horses. It comes from Old English mære, an evil spirit believed to sit on people's chests while they slept and give them bad dreams.

title: Your smallest bone is in your ear
body: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the body at roughly three millimetres long. It passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the fluid-filled inner ear.

title: Venus is hotter than Mercury
body: Mercury is closer to the Sun, but Venus has the hottest surface of any planet, about 464 degrees Celsius. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, while airless Mercury swings from about 420 degrees by day to minus 170 at night.

title: Land that no country wants
body: Bir Tawil, a desert area between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither. Two different border lines exist, and each country prefers the one that gives it the more valuable Halaib Triangle instead.

title: Most wasabi is really horseradish
body: Real wasabi is hard to grow and expensive, so most of the green paste served with sushi outside Japan is horseradish mixed with mustard and green colouring.

title: The platypus hunts with electricity
body: A platypus closes its eyes, ears and nose when it dives, yet still finds prey. Its bill carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that sense the tiny electric fields made by the muscles of shrimps and worms in the riverbed.

title: A Martian volcano 2.5 Everests tall
body: Olympus Mons rises about 21 kilometres, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest above sea level. Mars has no moving tectonic plates, so lava kept piling up over the same hotspot for an immensely long time.

title: In Italy a kindly witch brings presents
body: On the night before Epiphany, 6 January, Italian children await La Befana. The old woman on a broomstick fills stockings with sweets, or coal for naughty children.

title: Pencil "lead" has never been lead
body: Pencils are filled with graphite mixed with clay. When a large graphite deposit was found in England's Lake District in the 16th century, people mistook the shiny grey mineral for lead, and the name stuck.

title: Rafflesia has no leaves, stem or roots
body: Rafflesia, of the rainforests of South-East Asia, makes one of the largest flowers in the world, yet has no leaves, stem or roots. It lives hidden inside a vine as a parasite and only appears when its huge flower bursts through the bark.

title: Stretching a rubber band warms it up
body: Stretch a rubber band quickly and touch it to your lips: it feels warm, and it cools as it relaxes. Stretching lines up its tangled molecular chains, and that ordering releases heat.

title: Big Ben is kept on time with coins
body: The Great Clock at Westminster is fine-tuned by placing old penny coins on its pendulum. Adding one penny shifts the weight slightly and changes the clock's rate by about two-fifths of a second a day.

title: In Japan broken pots are mended with gold
body: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted with gold. Rather than hiding the cracks, it makes them shine, treating the damage as part of the object's history.

title: Baker's yeast was a genome pioneer
body: In 1996 baker's yeast became the first organism with a nucleus to have its entire genome sequenced. Many of its genes have close human equivalents, so the fungus that raises bread has taught us a great deal about our own cells.

title: Liquid oxygen is blue and magnetic
body: Cooled below minus 183 degrees Celsius, oxygen becomes a pale blue liquid that clings to the poles of a strong magnet. Oxygen molecules have unpaired electrons, which make them attracted to magnetic fields.

title: An ancient customer complaint survives in clay
body: Around 1750 BC a Babylonian named Nanni wrote an angry tablet to the merchant Ea-nasir about poor-quality copper and rude service. It is now in the British Museum and is often called the oldest known written complaint.

title: Orchestras agreed to tune to 440 Hz
body: For centuries the note A could vary widely from city to city. In 1939 an international conference in London recommended 440 vibrations a second, which became the usual standard.

title: Axolotls can regrow lost limbs
body: The axolotl, a salamander from the lakes around Mexico City, can regrow whole legs, parts of its heart and even its spinal cord. Cells at the wound turn back into a flexible state and rebuild the missing tissue without scarring.

title: Bees picked the most efficient shape
body: In 1999 mathematician Thomas Hales proved the honeycomb conjecture: hexagons divide a surface into equal cells using the least total wall length. Bees save wax by building hexagonal cells.

title: The busiest map spot is empty sea
body: Null Island is the nickname for 0° latitude, 0° longitude in the Gulf of Guinea. Faulty location data often defaults to those coordinates, so many mapping errors pile up on this imaginary island.

title: Winnie-the-Pooh was named after a real bear
body: Winnie was a black bear from Canada living at London Zoo, named after the city of Winnipeg. A. A. Milne's son Christopher Robin loved her and gave her name to his teddy bear.

title: The ocean's most common plant-like life
body: Prochlorococcus, a microbe too small to see even with many ordinary microscopes, was only discovered in 1988. Yet it is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth and produces a large share of the oxygen made in the sea.

title: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn
body: The unicorn has long been a symbol of Scotland's kings and still supports the royal coat of arms used in Scotland, wearing a chain. It is widely regarded as the country's national animal.

title: Sinterklaas arrives in the Netherlands by boat
body: Each November the Dutch Saint Nicholas is welcomed as he 'arrives from Spain' on a steamboat. His feast is celebrated with gifts on 5 December, the evening before St Nicholas's Day.

title: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver
body: Olympic gold medals are made mostly of silver and coated with gold. The last solid gold medals were awarded in 1912.

title: Your corneas breathe straight from the air
body: The cornea, the clear front of the eye, has no blood vessels, since they would cloud vision. Instead it takes most of its oxygen directly from the air, dissolved in the film of tears.

title: Why home-made ice cubes are cloudy
body: Ice cubes freeze from the outside in, pushing dissolved air and impurities towards the centre, where they get trapped as tiny bubbles. That is why the cloudiness gathers in the middle.

title: A Bristol clock has two minute hands
body: Before railways forced a national time, Bristol kept local time about ten minutes behind London. The Corn Exchange clock got a second minute hand to show both times.

title: The dot on an i has a name
body: The small dot above a lower-case i or j is called a tittle. The word is also thought to lie behind the phrase "to a T", meaning down to the smallest detail.

title: Tardigrades have survived open space
body: Tardigrades, or water bears, are tiny animals that can dry out and enter a state called cryptobiosis. In 2007 some were exposed to the vacuum and radiation of space on a satellite, and a number revived and reproduced afterwards.

title: Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side
body: Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees, so each pole points almost straight at the Sun for part of its 84-year orbit. That gives each pole roughly 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night.

title: A pirate who retired in peace
body: Ching Shih commanded a vast pirate confederation off southern China in the early 1800s. Instead of being defeated, she negotiated a surrender in 1810 that let her keep her fortune and live out her life.

title: Worcestershire sauce contains fish
body: The famous sauce gets part of its deep savoury taste from fermented anchovies. Other ingredients include vinegar, tamarind, molasses and onion.

title: Welwitschia grows just two leaves for life
body: Welwitschia, a desert plant of Namibia and Angola, produces only two leaves, which keep growing from the base for its whole life. Some plants are thought to be more than a thousand years old, their leaves torn by wind into ragged strips.

title: Trillions of ghostly particles pass through you
body: Every second, trillions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through your body, even at night when they come up through the Earth. They barely interact with matter, so almost all of them sail straight through.

title: An island that was never there
body: Sandy Island appeared on maps and even in online atlases for over a century, between Australia and New Caledonia. In 2012 scientists sailed to the spot and found only deep open ocean.

title: The safety pin paid off a debt
body: In 1849 the American inventor Walter Hunt twisted a piece of wire into a safety pin, reportedly in a few hours. He sold the patent for a few hundred dollars to settle a debt and never made more from it.

title: Lichens have survived a trip to space
body: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and algae or bacteria. In 2005 two lichen species spent about two weeks exposed to space on a satellite and resumed normal activity once back on Earth.

title: Only two elements are liquid at room temperature
body: Of all the elements, only mercury and bromine are liquid under everyday room conditions. Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid that gives off choking fumes, and its name comes from the Greek for stench.

title: In Bulgaria a nod can mean no
body: Traditionally Bulgarians nod their heads to say 'no' and shake them sideways to say 'yes'. The reversed gestures can easily confuse visitors.

title: A paint tube helped create Impressionism
body: In 1841 the American painter John Goffe Rand invented the squeezable metal paint tube. Artists could now carry ready-mixed paint outdoors, and Renoir is reported to have said Impressionism would not exist without it.

title: Whale songs spread like pop hits
body: Male humpback whales in a population all sing the same song, which slowly changes. Researchers have tracked new songs spreading from Australian waters eastward across the South Pacific, one population to the next, within a few years.

title: In the Monty Hall puzzle, always switch
body: With three doors, one prize and a host who opens a losing door, switching wins two times out of three. Your first pick is right only a third of the time, and the host's choice concentrates the rest on the other door.

title: Ramadan travels through all the seasons
body: The Islamic calendar follows the Moon and is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan begins earlier each year and moves through every season in roughly 33 years.

title: Ravel called his Boléro music without music
body: Ravel's Boléro repeats the same two melodies over a steady snare-drum rhythm, getting louder for about a quarter of an hour. Ravel himself described it as orchestral tissue without music.

title: The tongue taste map is a myth
body: Diagrams showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back come from a misreading of a German study of 1901. In fact taste buds on all parts of the tongue can detect all the basic tastes.

title: Earth's core rivals the Sun's surface
body: The temperature at Earth's inner core is estimated at over 5,000 degrees Celsius, roughly the same as the Sun's surface. The heat comes from Earth's formation and from radioactive decay.

title: Ancient Romans grabbed street food on the go
body: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, counters with built-in jars for serving hot food and drink. Many Romans lived in flats without kitchens, so takeaway meals were part of everyday life.

title: Peter Pan helps a children's hospital
body: In 1929 J. M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to Great Ormond Street Hospital in London. The hospital has received royalties from the story ever since, helped by a special act of Parliament.

title: Sloths can turn green
body: Sloths move so slowly that algae grow in grooves in their fur, giving them a greenish tint that helps camouflage them in the trees. Their fur also hosts moths, beetles and fungi, a whole tiny ecosystem.

title: A seashell does not hold the sea
body: The rushing sound when you hold a shell to your ear is surrounding noise echoing inside the shell. Its shape boosts some frequencies; a cup held to your ear does something similar.

title: A fake town that became real
body: Mapmakers invented Agloe, New York, in the 1930s as a 'trap' to catch copiers. Later a shop at the spot took the name Agloe, so for a time the made-up place really existed.

title: The marathon distance was set by royalty
body: At the 1908 London Olympics the marathon ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium, finishing in front of the royal box. That made it 42.195 km, which later became the official distance.

title: A tree known from fossils was found alive
body: The Wollemi pine was known from a fossil record going back many millions of years, then in 1994 a park ranger found living trees in a remote gorge near Sydney. Fewer than a hundred wild trees grow there.

title: The Sun is almost the whole Solar System
body: About 99.8 per cent of all the mass in the Solar System is in the Sun. All the planets, moons, asteroids and comets together make up only the tiny remainder, and Jupiter accounts for most of that.

title: The first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips
body: In Ireland and Scotland people carved faces into turnips and other root vegetables for Halloween. Emigrants to North America switched to the larger, easier-to-carve pumpkin.

title: "OK" began as a spelling joke
body: OK first appeared in a Boston newspaper in 1839 as short for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of all correct. Comic abbreviations were a fad at the time, and this was the one that survived.

title: The hat thrower fungus fires its spores
body: Pilobolus, which grows on dung, blasts its spore capsule more than two metres. The launch is among the fastest accelerations in nature, around 20,000 times gravity, so spores land on fresh grass where animals will eat them.

title: Mirrors swap front and back, not sides
body: A mirror does not truly swap left and right: your raised right hand appears on the same side. What it reverses is front to back. We just imagine walking round to stand where the reflection is.

title: In Thailand the year is 543 ahead
body: Thailand officially counts years in the Buddhist Era, which starts 543 years before the Western calendar. So AD 2000 was 2543 in Thailand.

title: "Pineapple" first meant pine cone
body: In English, pineapple originally meant the cone of a pine tree. When Europeans met the tropical fruit, its scaly skin reminded them of a pine cone, so the name moved across. Most languages call it ananas instead.

title: Sperm whales sleep standing upright
body: Sperm whales take short naps hanging vertically near the surface, heads up or down, completely still. Researchers discovered this in 2008 when they drifted into a group of sleeping whales that did not react to their boat.

title: Most ordinary matter is hydrogen
body: About three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe, by mass, is hydrogen, and most of the rest is helium. Nearly all heavier elements were made later inside stars.

title: A mighty warship that sank almost immediately
body: Sweden's warship Vasa capsized in 1628 on its maiden voyage, little more than a kilometre from where it set sail in Stockholm. It was top-heavy, and the cold brackish water preserved it so well that it was raised in 1961.

title: The first barcode scanned was on chewing gum
body: On 26 June 1974, in a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a packet of Wrigley's chewing gum became the first product sold using a barcode scanner. The packet is now kept at the Smithsonian.

title: Bright light makes some people sneeze
body: Many people, estimated at between a fifth and a third, sneeze when they step into bright sunlight. This 'photic sneeze reflex' runs in families and may come from signals in nerves of the eye and nose getting crossed.

title: Somewhere on Earth the wind is always still
body: The hairy ball theorem says you cannot comb a hairy sphere flat without a tuft or bald spot. Applied to wind, it means that at any moment there must be at least one point on Earth with no horizontal wind.

title: A country in all four hemispheres
body: Kiribati's islands straddle both the equator and the 180th meridian. That puts parts of it in the northern, southern, eastern and western hemispheres at once.

title: There is more than one Scream
body: Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream, including two paintings and two pastels, plus many prints. He often returned to his favourite images and reworked them.

title: Arctic terns chase an endless summer
body: Arctic terns breed in the far north and spend the northern winter near Antarctica, flying between them every year. Because they follow summer at both ends of the planet, they probably see more daylight than any other animal.

title: Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places
body: Rocks show that Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times, with north and south switching. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago, recorded in magnetised volcanic rock.

title: German children start school with sweet cones
body: On their first day of school, German children receive a Schultüte, a large paper cone filled with sweets and small gifts. It is meant to sweeten a big step in life.

title: An organ concert will last 639 years
body: In a church in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is playing John Cage's piece As Slow As Possible. It began in 2001 and is planned to end in 2640, so the chord changes are years apart.

title: The sensitive plant folds when touched
body: Mimosa pudica folds its leaflets within seconds of being touched. Cells at the base of each leaflet suddenly lose water, so the leaf collapses, which may startle grazing animals or knock off insects.

title: The sky is blue, not violet
body: Air scatters short-wavelength light most, so violet is scattered even more than blue. The sky looks blue because sunlight has less violet and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

title: Easter can fall on 35 different dates
body: Western Easter is the first Sunday after the church's spring full moon. It can land anywhere from 22 March to 25 April, depending on the lunar cycle.

title: The first Oscars ceremony was very short
body: The first Academy Awards in 1929 lasted only about 15 minutes. The winners had been announced three months earlier, so there was no suspense.

title: A slime mould redrew Tokyo's railways
body: In 2010 Japanese researchers placed oat flakes in the pattern of cities around Tokyo for a brainless slime mould. It linked them with a network strikingly similar to the region's rail lines. Slime moulds were once classed as fungi but are not.

title: Mark Twain arrived and left with Halley's Comet
body: Mark Twain was born in 1835, shortly after Halley's Comet passed close to the Sun, and predicted he would go out with it. He died in April 1910, the day after the comet's next closest approach to the Sun.

title: Einstein was offered a presidency
body: In 1952 Albert Einstein was invited to become President of Israel. He politely declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal with people and official functions.

title: Every Rubik's Cube is solvable in 20 moves
body: A Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible positions, yet in 2010 researchers proved that every one can be solved in 20 moves or fewer. Ernő Rubik first made the cube as a teaching tool.

title: Corals spawn together by moonlight
body: On the Great Barrier Reef, many coral species release their eggs and sperm on the same few nights after a full moon. Cued by water temperature, the Moon and sunset, the reef fills with drifting pink bundles like an underwater snowstorm.

title: Time runs faster at your head
body: Gravity slows time slightly, so clocks closer to the ground tick more slowly. In 2010 American scientists used atomic clocks to detect the difference over a height change of just 33 centimetres.

title: Venice stands on a forest of wooden posts
body: Much of Venice rests on millions of timber piles driven into the lagoon mud down to firmer clay. Kept waterlogged and away from oxygen, the wood has decayed only very slowly over centuries.

title: Most words for tea come from two sources
body: Languages that got tea overland, such as Hindi, Russian and Turkish, use a word like chai, from Mandarin cha. Those that got it by sea through Dutch traders, such as English and French, use tea, from the Min Chinese te.

title: Your brain is an energy guzzler
body: The brain makes up about 2 per cent of an adult's body weight but uses around a fifth of its energy at rest. Most of it goes on keeping neurons ready to fire by pumping charged particles across their membranes.

title: Why chopping onions makes you cry
body: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and starts reactions that release a sulfur compound gas. When the gas reaches your eyes it irritates them, and tear glands respond to wash it away.

title: Japanese families throw beans to chase away demons
body: At Setsubun in early February, people throw roasted soya beans while shouting 'Demons out, luck in!'. Many also eat one bean for each year of their age for good health.

title: Cashews are never sold in their shells
body: The cashew shell contains a caustic oil related to the irritant in poison ivy. The nuts are roasted or steamed and shelled before sale, which is why you never see them in their shells in shops.

title: Owls cannot move their eyes
body: An owl's eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in their sockets, so it cannot roll them. Instead it can turn its head about 270 degrees, helped by extra neck vertebrae and blood vessels arranged so that circulation is not cut off.

title: A nine-year-old named the googol
body: The word googol, meaning 1 followed by 100 zeros, was coined by Milton Sirotta, the young nephew of American mathematician Edward Kasner. Kasner popularised it in a 1940 book.

title: English weekdays honour Norse and Germanic gods
body: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are named after Tiw, Woden, Thor and Frigg. They replaced Roman gods: French still has mardi for Mars and mercredi for Mercury.

title: Pen caps have a hole for safety
body: The small hole in the top of many pen caps lets air through if a child accidentally swallows one. It was added to reduce the risk of choking.

title: Butterflies taste with their feet
body: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet that work on contact. A female lands on a leaf and 'tastes' it to check whether it will feed her caterpillars before she lays her eggs.

title: Mauna Kea beats Everest from base to top
body: Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is about 10,000 metres tall, more than Everest's height above sea level. Most of it lies hidden beneath the Pacific.

title: Isaac Newton chased forgers for the Royal Mint
body: Later in life Isaac Newton became Warden, then Master, of the Royal Mint. He threw himself into the job, gathering evidence against counterfeiters and helping prosecute them.

title: Vermeer's pearl-earring girl is not a portrait
body: Vermeer's famous painting is a tronie, a Dutch study of a face, expression or costume rather than a picture of a particular person. Nobody knows who modelled for it.

title: Mushrooms make vitamin D in sunlight
body: Like our skin, mushrooms produce vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light. They contain ergosterol, which sunlight converts into vitamin D2, so mushrooms left gills up in the sun gain much more of it.

title: Why cut apples turn brown
body: When an apple is cut, an enzyme in its cells meets oxygen in the air and turns natural compounds into brown pigments. Lemon juice slows this because its acid hinders the enzyme.

title: Earth's farthest-out peak is not Everest
body: The summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth farthest from its centre. The planet bulges at the equator, so this Andean volcano sticks out further than Everest.

title: You play the theremin without touching it
body: The theremin, invented by the Russian Léon Theremin around 1920, has two antennas. Moving one hand near each changes the pitch and volume, so the player never touches the instrument.

title: Parrotfish help make white sand beaches
body: Parrotfish bite off algae-covered coral with beak-like teeth and grind it up with a second set of teeth in their throats. The coral passes out as fine white sand, and on many tropical reefs they produce a large share of the beach.

title: One Mercury day lasts two Mercury years
body: From sunrise to sunrise takes about 176 Earth days on Mercury, while a trip round the Sun takes only 88. Its slow spin and fast orbit combine so the Sun crawls across its sky extremely slowly.

title: Scots welcome the first visitor of the year
body: At Hogmanay the first person to cross the threshold after midnight, the 'first-foot', sets the year's luck. A tall dark stranger carrying coal, shortbread or salt is traditionally the luckiest.

title: The Jaws shark was nicknamed Bruce
body: The film crew named the mechanical shark Bruce after Steven Spielberg's lawyer. It kept breaking down in salt water, so the shark appears less than planned, which made the film more suspenseful.

title: You have about as many microbes as cells
body: The old claim that bacteria outnumber our own cells ten to one was revised in 2016. A careful count found the numbers are roughly equal, at a few tens of trillions each.

title: A custard that turns solid when punched
body: A mix of cornflour and water flows like a liquid when stirred gently but becomes hard when hit or squeezed suddenly. The starch grains cannot slide past each other fast enough and jam together.

title: There was no year zero
body: In the usual Western count, 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1. The system was devised in the 6th century, before the idea of zero had reached Europe.

title: Monopoly began as a warning against monopolies
body: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 by Lizzie Magie. She designed it to show how landlords grow rich while tenants grow poor.

title: Naked mole-rats live remarkably long lives
body: Naked mole-rats, from the dry lands of East Africa, are about the size of a mouse yet can live for more than 30 years and rarely develop cancer. They live underground in colonies with a single breeding queen, like bees.

title: Tin can crumble in the cold
body: Below about 13 degrees Celsius, shiny metallic tin can slowly turn into a crumbly grey powder called tin pest. The atoms rearrange into a different, less dense crystal structure that falls apart.

title: Australia once fought a war against emus
body: In 1932 soldiers with machine guns were sent to Western Australia to cull emus damaging wheat crops. The fast, scattering birds proved so hard to hit that the 'Great Emu War' is remembered as a failure.

title: A lady was once a bread-kneader
body: "Lady" comes from Old English hlǣfdīge, probably meaning "loaf-kneader", and "lord" from hlāfweard, "loaf-guardian". Both words seem to tie the heads of an Anglo-Saxon household to its bread.

title: Coffee flowers give bees a caffeine buzz
body: Coffee and citrus flowers lace their nectar with small amounts of caffeine. A 2013 study found bees that drank it remembered the flower's scent much better, so they were more likely to return and pollinate it.

title: Some infinities are bigger than others
body: Georg Cantor showed in the 1870s and 1890s that there are more real numbers than whole numbers, even though both are infinite. No list, however long, can include every decimal number.

title: An island that switches country every six months
body: Pheasant Island in the river Bidasoa is ruled by Spain for half the year and France for the other half. The shared arrangement dates from the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on the island.

title: Fortune cookies are probably Japanese, not Chinese
body: Fortune cookies are almost unknown in China. Researchers have traced them to Japanese crackers made near Kyoto, which Japanese immigrants brought to California in the early 20th century.

title: Fairy rings are fungi growing outwards
body: Rings of mushrooms in grass, once blamed on dancing fairies, mark the edge of a fungus spreading out from a central point. As it uses up nutrients in the middle, only the outer edge keeps fruiting, so the ring widens each year.

title: Hailstones are layered like onions
body: Cut a big hailstone in half and you often see rings. As it is swept through a storm cloud it passes through regions with more or less supercooled water, adding layers of clear and cloudy ice. Repeated up-and-down trips were once thought necessary, but are not.

title: Ukrainian Christmas trees wear spider webs
body: Some Ukrainians decorate trees with spider-web ornaments. A folk tale tells of a poor widow's bare tree that spiders covered in webs which turned to silver and gold in the morning light.

title: Superglue was rejected for being too sticky
body: Chemist Harry Coover first made the glue in 1942 while trying to make clear plastic gun sights. It stuck to everything, so it was set aside, until he rediscovered it years later and saw its value.

title: Deep-sea vents host life without sunlight
body: In 1977 scientists exploring off the Galápagos found giant tubeworms, clams and crabs around hot springs on the dark sea floor. Their food chain starts with bacteria that draw energy from chemicals in the vent water, not from sunlight.

title: Mint feels cold without being cold
body: Menthol in mint triggers the same nerve sensors in your mouth that respond to cold. The brain gets a cold signal even though the temperature has not changed.

title: The year 1900 was not a leap year
body: Century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 was not. This rule keeps the calendar close to the true solar year of about 365.2422 days.

title: Leonardo's Last Supper began fading quickly
body: Instead of painting on wet plaster, as in true fresco, Leonardo painted The Last Supper on a dry wall so he could work slowly. The paint did not bond well and started flaking within his lifetime.

title: A single gene decides your earwax type
body: Earwax comes in a wet, sticky type and a dry, flaky type, decided by a single gene. The dry type is most common in East Asia, while the wet type predominates in Europe and Africa.

title: The Moon drifts away at fingernail speed
body: Lasers bounced off mirrors left by Apollo crews show the Moon moving away by about 3.8 centimetres a year. Tides on Earth steal a little of our planet's spin and pass that energy to the Moon, pushing it outwards.

title: A medieval traveller who outdid Marco Polo
body: Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, spent nearly 30 years travelling in the 1300s, reaching West Africa, India and China. His journeys covered far more ground than Marco Polo's, and he dictated them in a famous book, the Rihla.

title: The tuning fork was invented by a trumpeter
body: John Shore, a trumpeter who played for Handel, invented the tuning fork in 1711. He reportedly joked that it was his "pitch-fork".

title: Crows remember human faces
body: In experiments in Seattle, researchers in masks trapped and released crows. Years later the birds still scolded anyone wearing those masks, and crows that had never been trapped joined in, showing they learn who is dangerous from each other.

title: A glass drop that resists a hammer
body: Prince Rupert's drops form when molten glass falls into cold water. Their round head can survive a hammer blow, yet snapping the thin tail makes the whole drop burst into powder, as locked-in stresses are released.

title: Nepal's flag is not a rectangle
body: Nepal's national flag is made of two stacked pennants, giving it a double-pointed shape. Every other national flag is a rectangle or a square.

title: India's first talking film started a tradition
body: Alam Ara, released in 1931, was India's first sound film. It included several songs, beginning the tradition of music being central to Indian cinema.

title: A 2,000-year-old seed grew into a tree
body: In 2005 scientists planted a date palm seed found at Masada, the ancient fortress in Israel, and radiocarbon dated to about 2,000 years old. It sprouted, and the palm, nicknamed Methuselah, has grown into a healthy tree.

title: Table salt comes from two dangerous elements
body: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous gas. Combined, they form sodium chloride, a stable compound we sprinkle on chips.

title: Swedes watch Donald Duck every Christmas Eve
body: Since 1959 Swedish television has shown a Disney cartoon special at 3 pm on Christmas Eve. Watching 'Kalle Anka' with the family has become a beloved ritual.

title: Scrabble scores come from counting newspaper letters
body: Alfred Butts, who invented Scrabble, decided how many tiles each letter should have, and their points, by counting how often letters appeared in newspapers such as The New York Times.

title: Some fungi seem to feed on radiation
body: Black fungi rich in melanin grow on the walls of the ruined Chernobyl reactor. Laboratory studies found some such fungi grew faster when exposed to radiation, suggesting they may harvest its energy, though how is still studied.

title: 1729 is not as dull as it looks
body: When G. H. Hardy called his taxi number 1729 dull, Srinivasa Ramanujan replied that it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two ways: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed, and 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.

title: Japan's era name came from ancient poetry
body: Japan names years after imperial eras. 'Reiwa', which began in 2019, was the first era name taken from a Japanese classic, the poetry collection Man'yōshū, rather than from Chinese texts.

title: Quarantine means forty days
body: "Quarantine" comes from Venetian quaranta giorni, forty days. During medieval plague outbreaks, ships arriving at Venice had to wait that long before passengers and crew could come ashore.

title: Starfish have an eye on each arm
body: At the tip of each arm, many sea stars have a small red eye made of dozens of light-sensing units. It cannot see detail or colour, but lets the animal make out large shapes, such as the reef where it lives.

title: Saharan dust feeds the Amazon
body: Satellite studies show winds carry millions of tonnes of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic every year. It contains phosphorus, a nutrient that helps replace what heavy rains wash out of Amazon soils.

title: A Roman emperor who preferred cabbages
body: Diocletian became one of the few Roman emperors to retire, stepping down in 305. When later urged to return to power, he reportedly said that anyone who saw the cabbages he grew would not ask him to.

title: Nutmeg and mace grow on the same fruit
body: Nutmeg is the seed of the nutmeg tree's fruit, and mace is the lacy red covering wrapped around that seed. They are dried separately and taste similar, but mace is more delicate.

title: Each eye has a blind spot
body: Where the optic nerve leaves the back of each eye there are no light-sensing cells, so there is a gap in your vision. You never notice it because the other eye covers it and the brain fills in the hole.

title: Water can be ice, liquid and vapour together
body: At 0.01 degrees Celsius and a pressure under 1 per cent of normal air pressure, water reaches its triple point. There ice, liquid water and water vapour can all exist together in stable balance, melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing at equal rates.

title: A Roman road map nearly seven metres long
body: The Tabula Peutingeriana, a medieval copy of a Roman road map, is a scroll about 6.7 metres long but only about a third of a metre tall. It squashes the empire into a strip to show routes and distances, not true shapes.

title: "Escalator" was once a brand name
body: Escalator was a trademark of the Otis Elevator Company. People used it so widely for any moving staircase that in 1950 it was ruled a generic word, and Otis lost the exclusive right to it.

title: Japanese monkeys enjoy hot baths
body: At Jigokudani in Japan, macaques soak in hot springs during the snowy winter. A 2018 study found that bathing lowered levels of stress hormones in the monkeys, suggesting it helps them conserve energy and stay calm in the cold.

title: Pluto has not orbited once since its discovery
body: Pluto was discovered in 1930, but it takes about 248 Earth years to circle the Sun. It will not complete its first full orbit since being spotted until the 2170s.

title: A Tibetan greeting with the tongue
body: Traditionally some Tibetans greet others by showing their tongue. A popular story links it to a cruel 9th-century king, Langdarma, said to have had a black tongue, so a pink one proved good intentions.

title: A painting shredded itself after being sold
body: In 2018 Banksy's Girl with Balloon passed through a shredder hidden in its frame moments after it was sold at auction in London. The half-shredded work was renamed Love is in the Bin.

title: A frog that survives being frozen
body: In winter the North American wood frog can let about two-thirds of its body water freeze, with no heartbeat or breathing. Sugar flooding its cells limits the damage, and in spring it thaws and hops away.

title: Dry spaghetti rarely snaps in two
body: Bend a dry spaghetti strand from both ends and it usually breaks into three or more pieces. The first break sends a vibration back along each half, causing extra breaks. Twisting it first can make it snap in two.

title: Sixty minutes comes from ancient Babylon
body: Our 60 minutes and 60 seconds come from the base-60 counting used in ancient Mesopotamia. Sixty divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30.

title: West African drums can talk
body: Hourglass-shaped talking drums have cords that the player squeezes to change the pitch. Because Yoruba and other West African languages are tonal, the drums can copy the melody of speech and send messages.

title: Japan has a national fungus
body: Koji mould, Aspergillus oryzae, is used to make soy sauce, miso and sake. It is so important to Japanese cooking that the Brewing Society of Japan named it the country's 'national fungus' in 2006.

title: Firework colours come from metals
body: Strontium gives fireworks red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow. Heat excites the metals' electrons, and each element gives off light at its own characteristic colours as they settle back.

title: England had a nine-day queen
body: Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed Queen of England in July 1553 but was replaced by Mary I just over a week later. Her claim lacked support, and the country swung behind Henry VIII's daughter.

title: Godzilla is part gorilla, part whale
body: Godzilla's Japanese name, Gojira, blends gorira (gorilla) and kujira (whale). The monster first appeared in a Japanese film in 1954.

title: The panda's thumb is not a thumb
body: Giant pandas grip bamboo with what looks like a sixth finger. It is actually an enlarged wrist bone covered in a fleshy pad, which works against the other fingers to hold stems while the panda strips them.

title: The magic number 6174
body: Take a four-digit number with at least two different digits, arrange its digits largest-first and smallest-first, and subtract. Repeat, and you reach 6174 within seven steps, as Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar found.

title: 'Here be dragons' is rare on old maps
body: Despite its fame, the Latin phrase 'hic sunt dracones' is known from almost no historical maps, most famously the Hunt–Lenox Globe of about 1510. Old mapmakers more often drew sea monsters than wrote warnings.

title: In kabaddi you must chant without breathing
body: In the South Asian sport kabaddi, a raider runs into the other team's half while chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" without pausing. The chant proves the raider is holding a single breath.

title: Most deep-sea animals make their own light
body: Studies of animals filmed off California found roughly three-quarters of those living in the open ocean can produce light. They use it to lure prey, find mates, or hide their silhouette against the faint light from above.

title: Some sand dunes sing
body: Certain dunes, such as Mingsha Shan near Dunhuang in China, make a loud booming hum when sand slides down them. Avalanching grains move in step, producing a low note that can last for minutes.

title: Māori greet by pressing noses together
body: The hongi is a traditional Māori greeting in which two people press their noses and foreheads together. It symbolises sharing the breath of life.

title: A window is a "wind eye"
body: The English word window comes from Old Norse vindauga, literally "wind eye". Early Scandinavian houses had simple holes in the roof or wall that let out smoke and let in the wind.

title: You cannot tickle yourself
body: When you move, your brain predicts the touch that will follow and dampens your response to it. Tickling yourself is therefore never a surprise, so it does not feel ticklish.

title: Why metal feels colder than wood
body: A metal spoon and a wooden one in the same room are equally warm, yet the metal feels colder. Metal conducts heat away from your skin much faster, and your nerves sense that heat loss.

title: Roman hours changed length with the seasons
body: Romans split daylight into 12 hours whatever the time of year. So a summer daytime hour was much longer than a winter one.

title: A 12-year-old boy saved the vanilla industry
body: In 1841 on Réunion, Edmond Albius, an enslaved boy of 12, worked out how to pollinate vanilla flowers by hand. Outside Mexico the plant had no natural pollinators, and his method is still used today.

title: Dung beetles navigate by the Milky Way
body: Some South African dung beetles roll their balls in straight lines even on moonless nights. In a 2013 study in a planetarium, they only kept their course when the band of the Milky Way was visible, the first animals shown to use it.

title: Total eclipses rely on a cosmic coincidence
body: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so both look almost the same size in our sky. That is why the Moon can just cover the Sun's disc during a total eclipse.

title: Athenians voted with broken pottery
body: In ancient Athens citizens could banish a powerful politician for ten years by scratching his name on a pottery shard called an ostrakon. That practice gives us the word 'ostracism'.

title: A woman on a tram invented the wiper
body: On a snowy trip to New York, Mary Anderson saw a tram driver lean out of the window to clear his windscreen. She designed a hand-operated wiper, patented in 1903.

title: The potato is a tomato's close cousin
body: Potatoes and tomatoes belong to the same genus, Solanum, and their leaves and flowers look alike. The sweet potato, despite its name, is from a different family altogether and is related to morning glory.

title: Scientists slowed light to cycling speed
body: In 1999 a team led by Danish physicist Lene Hau slowed light to about 17 metres per second by sending it through an ultra-cold cloud of sodium atoms, roughly the speed of a fast cyclist.

title: California was once drawn as an island
body: For much of the 1600s and 1700s many European maps showed California as a huge island. The mistake spread from copied maps until Spanish explorers confirmed it was connected to the mainland.

title: Prussian blue was discovered by accident
body: Around 1706 a Berlin colour-maker trying to make a red got a deep blue instead, because one of his ingredients was contaminated. Prussian blue is often called the first modern synthetic pigment.

title: Mushrooms create their own breeze
body: Mushrooms release water vapour that cools the air around them. A 2016 study showed this makes small air currents that lift spores out from under the cap, so they can spread even when the air is still.

title: An element was named after a living chemist
body: In 1997 element 106 was officially named seaborgium after American chemist Glenn Seaborg while he was still alive. Only one other element, oganesson, has been named after a person living at the time.

title: A Polish Christmas table has a spare seat
body: At the Christmas Eve supper, Wigilia, many Polish families set an extra place. It is kept for an unexpected guest or wanderer, so nobody is turned away.

title: The erhu's bow is trapped between its strings
body: The Chinese erhu has just two strings and no fingerboard. Its bow hair passes between the two strings, so the bow cannot be removed and the player plays by pushing it against one string or the other.

title: Clownfish can change from male to female
body: Clownfish live in small groups in a sea anemone, led by one large female and her male mate. All start as males, and if the female dies her mate becomes female and the next largest fish takes his place.

title: A Chinese fraction nailed pi for centuries
body: In the 5th century, Zu Chongzhi gave 355/113 as an approximation of pi, correct to six decimal places. For almost 900 years afterwards, no one is known to have calculated a more precise value.

title: Benjamin Franklin's daylight-saving idea was a joke
body: Franklin's 1784 essay about Parisians wasting candles was satire. Modern daylight saving was proposed by New Zealand insect collector George Hudson in 1895, who wanted more evening light for bug hunting.

title: The first animated feature film was Argentine
body: El Apóstol, made in Argentina by Quirino Cristiani in 1917, is considered the first feature-length animated film. Made with paper cut-outs, it is now lost; no copy is known to survive.

title: Wrinkly fingers in water are deliberate
body: Fingers wrinkle in the bath because nerves make blood vessels in the fingertips narrow, not just because skin soaks up water. Fingers with damaged nerves do not wrinkle, and some studies suggest the ridges improve grip on wet objects.

title: Snow can be pink
body: In summer, snowfields in mountains and polar regions can turn pink or red, called watermelon snow. It is caused by cold-loving algae with a red pigment that protects them from strong sunlight.

title: The Terracotta Army was once brightly painted
body: The clay soldiers guarding China's First Emperor were originally coloured with vivid paints. Once exposed to dry air after excavation, the lacquer beneath the paint can curl within 15 seconds and flake off within about four minutes.

title: Cricket's Ashes began as a joke obituary
body: After Australia beat England at the Oval in London in 1882, the Sporting Times printed a mock obituary for English cricket, saying its body would be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia.

title: Hippos make their own sunscreen
body: Hippos ooze a reddish fluid often called 'blood sweat', though it is neither blood nor sweat. Its red and orange pigments absorb sunlight, and studies suggest they also hold back the growth of some bacteria.

title: A moon bigger than the planet Mercury
body: Jupiter's moon Ganymede is about 5,270 kilometres across, wider than the planet Mercury. It is less massive, though, because it is made largely of ice and rock rather than Mercury's dense iron.

title: Sailors mapped the sea with sticks
body: Marshall Islands navigators made charts of sticks and shells that showed ocean swells and how they bend around islands. They memorised them on land rather than carrying them aboard.

title: An island where people talk by whistling
body: On La Gomera in the Canary Islands, people can whistle Spanish across deep valleys using Silbo Gomero. The whistles copy the rise and fall of speech, and the language is taught in island schools and listed by UNESCO.

title: Wheat has a bigger genome than you
body: Bread wheat's genome is about five times larger than the human genome. It formed when three different ancestral grasses hybridised, so each wheat cell carries six sets of chromosomes, two from each of those species.

title: A hammer and feather fell together
body: In 1971 Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon, and they landed together. With no air resistance, gravity accelerates every object equally.

title: Guatemalans fly giant kites for the dead
body: On All Saints' Day in Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez, people fly huge, colourful kites over cemeteries. The kites are said to carry messages to loved ones who have died.

title: Tonic water glows under ultraviolet light
body: Tonic water glows bright blue under a black light. The quinine that gives it its bitter taste absorbs invisible ultraviolet light and gives it back as visible blue light.

title: Some fungi lasso worms
body: Certain soil fungi set traps for tiny worms called nematodes. One kind forms rings that swell in a fraction of a second when a worm pushes through, gripping it tight before the fungus grows inside to feed.

title: Fluorine can even react with a noble gas
body: Fluorine is so reactive that it combines with almost every element. In 1962 chemists showed that xenon reacts directly with fluorine to form xenon tetrafluoride, ending the belief that noble gases never react.

title: The Soviet Union tried a five-day week
body: From 1929 the USSR used a continuous working week in which workers had staggered days off. It aimed to keep factories running non-stop but disrupted family life and was dropped by 1940.

title: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king
body: Bluetooth wireless technology is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united Danish tribes. Its logo combines the runes for his initials, H and B.

title: A sponge can rebuild itself from crumbs
body: In 1907 a biologist pressed living sponges through fine cloth, breaking them into separate cells. Over the next days the cells crawled back together and reorganised into new working sponges, which have no organs, nerves or muscles.

title: Brahmagupta wrote the rules for zero
body: In 628 CE the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta treated zero as a number in its own right and set out rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with it. Our modern zero descends from this Indian tradition.

title: Medieval scholars knew the Earth was round
body: The idea that people in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was flat is largely a 19th-century myth. Educated Europeans followed ancient Greek writers who had shown the Earth is a sphere.

title: An 18-year-old's mistake made the colour mauve fashionable
body: In 1856 the chemistry student William Perkin was trying to make the malaria drug quinine and produced a purple dye instead. Mauveine was the first synthetic dye and set off a craze for mauve clothes.

title: Your nostrils take turns
body: Through the day, one nostril is usually more open than the other, and the roles swap every few hours. This 'nasal cycle' is controlled by the nervous system and may let each side of the nose rest and recover.

title: Why there are two high tides a day
body: The Moon's gravity raises a bulge of ocean on the side facing it and another on the far side, where the Earth is pulled away from the water. Earth turns through both bulges each day.
