title: A country with two princes, one French
body: Andorra's two heads of state are co-princes: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain. The arrangement goes back to a medieval agreement made in 1278.

title: The black spot on a tabla tunes it
body: The dark circle on Indian tabla drums is a hardened paste of iron filings and flour. Its extra weight makes the drum produce clear, musical overtones, as the physicist C. V. Raman studied.

title: Zebra stripes confuse biting flies
body: One leading explanation for zebra stripes is defence against flies. In a 2019 experiment, horseflies circled horses wearing striped coats but often failed to land, apparently unable to judge their approach against the pattern.

title: Honey can keep for a very long time
body: Sealed honey resists spoiling for a very long time. It contains very little water and is acidic, so microbes cannot grow in it, and an enzyme added by bees produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide.

title: Spain's tooth fairy is a mouse
body: Children in Spain and much of Latin America leave lost teeth for Ratoncito Pérez. The writer Luis Coloma created the mouse's story in 1894 for the young King Alfonso XIII.

title: James Bond was named after a bird expert
body: Ian Fleming, a keen birdwatcher, borrowed the name James Bond from the American author of a guide to the birds of the West Indies. He wanted a name that sounded as plain as possible.

title: Ripe oranges can be green
body: An orange's colour comes from cool nights breaking down the green chlorophyll in its peel. In warm climates ripe oranges can stay green, which is why some countries sell perfectly ripe green ones.

title: Seeing 2.5 million years into the past
body: On a dark night the Andromeda Galaxy is visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge. It lies about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light reaching you left it before modern humans existed.

title: The Maya calendar never predicted 2012's end
body: 21 December 2012 simply marked the end of a 13th b'ak'tun cycle in the Maya Long Count. Like a car's odometer rolling over, the count just carried on.

title: Snakes and ladders was a lesson in morals
body: Snakes and ladders comes from ancient India, where it taught that good deeds lead upwards and bad ones lead down. Ladders stood for virtues such as generosity and snakes for vices.

title: Cholesterol drugs began with a mould
body: In the 1970s Japanese scientist Akira Endo screened thousands of fungi and found a Penicillium mould making a substance that blocked cholesterol production. It led to statins, which became some of the most widely prescribed medicines in the world.

title: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
body: A lightning bolt heats the air to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the Sun's surface. This sudden heating makes the air expand explosively, which we hear as thunder.

title: The first named author was a priestess
body: Enheduanna, high priestess and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, composed hymns around 2300 BC and named herself in them. She is widely regarded as the earliest author in history known by name.

title: "Serendipity" comes from an old Persian tale
body: Horace Walpole coined serendipity in 1754, inspired by The Three Princes of Serendip. In the story, the princes keep making lucky discoveries by accident. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka.

title: Box jellyfish have 24 eyes
body: Box jellyfish carry 24 eyes in four clusters, and some even have lenses that focus images. Despite having no brain, they use them to steer around obstacles and navigate towards mangrove roots.

title: Four colours are enough for any map
body: Any flat map can be coloured with only four colours so that no neighbouring regions match. Proved in 1976 by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, it was the first major theorem proved with heavy computer help.

title: The world map that is a clay tablet
body: The Babylonian Map of the World, made around the 6th century BC, shows Babylon inside a ring-shaped ocean. It is one of the oldest surviving attempts to draw the whole known world.

title: Pound cake was named after its recipe
body: The original pound cake used a pound each of flour, butter, sugar and eggs. The simple equal-weight ratio made it easy to remember, and the French call a similar cake quatre-quarts, 'four quarters'.

title: Humans are built for long-distance running
body: Few animals can outlast humans over long distances in heat, thanks to our sweating skin and springy legs. San hunters in the Kalahari have been recorded running down antelope in the midday heat until the animals overheat.

title: The smell of rain has a name
body: The earthy smell after rain on dry ground is called petrichor, a word coined by two Australian scientists in 1964. Part of it is geosmin, made by soil bacteria, which our noses can detect in tiny traces.

title: Irish tradition lets women propose on leap day
body: According to an old Irish legend, St Brigid asked St Patrick to let women propose marriage, and 29 February became the day for it. Some later versions say a man who refuses owes a gift.

title: The first stethoscope was a paper tube
body: In 1816 the French doctor René Laennec felt it improper to press his ear to a young woman's chest. He rolled some paper into a tube and found it carried her heartbeat clearly, so he built a wooden version.

title: Cats cannot taste sweetness
body: Cats lack a working version of one of the two genes needed for the sweet taste receptor, so sugar holds no appeal for them. As strict meat-eaters, their ancestors had no need to detect it, and the gene broke down.

title: Why spilled coffee dries as a ring
body: As a coffee drop dries, its edge stays pinned while liquid evaporates fastest there. Liquid flows outwards to replace it, carrying coffee particles that pile up at the edge, leaving a dark ring.

title: An Irish tomb catches the winter sunrise
body: Newgrange, built around 3200 BC and older than Giza's pyramids, has a roof box above its entrance. For a few days around the winter solstice, dawn light shines down the passage into the inner chamber.

title: Ancient Greek statues were brightly painted
body: The white marble statues we admire were once painted in vivid colours. Traces of pigment, some visible only under ultraviolet light, show that the paint simply wore away over the centuries.

title: The corpse flower warms itself up
body: The titan arum of Sumatra blooms for only a day or two and smells of rotting meat to attract beetles and flies. Its central spike heats up close to human body temperature, which helps the smell rise and spread through the forest.

title: The Sun is really white, not yellow
body: Seen from space, sunlight is essentially white, a mix of all colours. It looks yellow or orange from the ground because our atmosphere scatters away some of the blue light, especially when the Sun is low.

title: Egyptian tomb builders took days off for beer
body: Records from the workers' village of Deir el-Medina list why men missed work, including illness, a scorpion sting and brewing beer. These skilled, paid craftsmen built royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

title: "Amazing Grace" was written by an ex-slave trader
body: The hymn was written by John Newton, who had captained slave ships before becoming a clergyman. He later spoke out against the slave trade and supported its abolition.

title: Blue cheese gets its veins from mould
body: The blue streaks in Roquefort and Stilton are a harmless mould, Penicillium roqueforti. Cheesemakers pierce the cheese with needles to let in air, and the mould grows along the channels, adding its sharp flavour.

title: Neptune was found with pen and paper
body: Uranus was drifting off its predicted path, so Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unseen planet must be. In 1846 Johann Galle pointed a telescope there and found Neptune within about a degree of the prediction.

title: A Welsh village name invented to attract tourists
body: Llanfairpwllgwyngyll in Anglesey gained its 58-letter name in the 1860s. Locals stretched it to draw visitors arriving by the new railway, and it worked.

title: Toy Story was the first all-computer film
body: Released in 1995, Pixar's Toy Story was the first feature film made entirely with computer animation. Every frame was drawn by computers, taking hours each to render.

title: Dolphins call each other by name
body: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own 'signature whistle'. Experiments show dolphins respond when they hear their own whistle copied, much as we turn when someone calls our name.

title: Temple bells ring 108 times at New Year
body: On New Year's Eve, Japanese Buddhist temples strike their bells 108 times in a ritual called joya no kane. Each strike symbolises driving out one of 108 worldly desires.

title: Football's red and yellow cards copy traffic lights
body: English referee Ken Aston thought of the cards while waiting at traffic lights in London. They were introduced at the 1970 World Cup so players who spoke different languages could understand the referee.

title: Blue eyes contain no blue pigment
body: Blue eyes have very little pigment in the front layer of the iris. The blue comes from light scattering off the iris tissue, much as the sky looks blue, which is why eye colour can seem to shift in different lighting.

title: Shakespeare and Cervantes did not die together
body: Both are often said to have died on 23 April 1616, but Spain used the Gregorian calendar and England the older Julian one. Shakespeare actually died about ten days after Cervantes.

title: A disaster is a bad star
body: "Disaster" comes from Italian disastro, meaning ill-starred. It reflects an old belief that misfortune came when the stars and planets were in an unlucky position.
